rows.response:
**Don't push through today's session. Skip any loaded lower-body work, and screen him before he trains at all.** The lower-body part is my coaching judgement from general knowledge. I haven't pulled course pages for it, so I'm not citing any.

**What's most likely**

Three weeks off, then a first session at his old loads, then trouble walking the next day. That fits severe delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) from returning at full load. It's the usual result of skipping a ramp-up after a layoff. Detraining costs strength and work capacity faster than people expect, and the eccentric-heavy work does the damage. Normal DOMS peaks around 24–72 hours, so today may not be the worst of it.

**Screen first, because "can barely walk" is more than normal soreness**

This is not yours to diagnose or clear. Ask him these before anything else:
- Is his urine dark (tea or cola coloured)?
- Is there marked swelling or tightness in the legs?
- Is the pain out of proportion to the session, or sharp and localized rather than diffuse muscle ache?
- Is he unusually weak, nauseous, or feeling generally unwell?

If any answer is yes, send him to a doctor today and don't train him. Exertional rhabdomyolysis can follow an overly hard return after time off. If he reports sharp or localized pain, treat it as an injury symptom and refer out as well.

**Default for today, if the screen is clean (diffuse ache, no red flags)**

- **No loaded lower-body work.** Heavy squats, lunges and hinges on sore, damaged muscle add more damage without much training benefit.
- **Train around it if he can do so comfortably.** Upper-body work at a reduced load is fine.
- **Add easy movement.** Walking, a bike or other low-load movement, and gentle mobility are fine if they feel better as he moves. Stop if they don't.
- **Cancel the session if he can't move comfortably.** Don't force it, and reschedule.

**Resuming the lower body**

Bring it back only when he can walk normally and stairs are tolerable. Restart at roughly 60–70% of his old loads, with reps in reserve and no grinding sets. Progress about 5–10% a week as long as soreness stays manageable and clears within about 48 hours.

**For your records**

If he's on a REVL phase or a written plan, log the layoff and the soreness response. Re-baseline his loads before the next heavy block. I haven't touched any client files, since you haven't named him.

If he says yes to any of the red-flag questions, tell me and I'll help you word the referral.

**Default plan, assuming she is in Volume or Rebuild.** I don't yet know her phase, her track or which weekday is which REVL session, so treat this as provisional.

## The problem to fix first
REVL 5x plus PT 3x is 8 sessions in 7 days, so she will have no full rest day. REVL also trains squat and hinge on almost every day, and pressing and pulling often. More compound volume would just pile on fatigue. For size, the PT sessions should add direct hypertrophy work on what REVL under-serves:
- horizontal and vertical pulling
- upper back and rear delts
- lateral delts
- arms
- calves
- low-fatigue leg isolation

*(General approach: REVL reference §6a, §14 "build muscle" row, example E. Applied from the course, not stated by it.)*

## Dosing for all three sessions
- **Sets and reps:** 3–4 sets of 8–15 reps, with 60–90 s rest on compounds and 30–60 s on isolation. This is the hypertrophy band from Table 9-12, which the REVL reference digest cites at p16. I haven't re-verified the page this turn.
- **Effort:** RIR 1–3 on upper work and RIR 2–3 on lower work. Do not train to failure, because her cumulative fatigue is already high. This is general knowledge, not from the ISA course.
- **Lower-body choices:** machine and isolation work only. No axial loading, no heavy hinge and no deep loaded stretches. Long-muscle eccentric damage would carry into the next REVL day.
- **Progression trigger (all three sessions):** double progression. When she hits the top of the rep range on every set at the target RIR for two consecutive sessions, add about 5% load and restart at the bottom of the range. Both the 2-for-2 rule and the ~5% increment come from the course digest (Wk07 Ch11 p7, p20). I haven't re-verified the pages this turn.

|---|---|
| Chest-supported row | 4 × 8–12 |
| Lat pulldown (neutral grip) | 3 × 10–12 |
| Cable or machine rear-delt fly | 3 × 12–15 |
| Incline DB curl | 3 × 10–12 |
| Hammer curl | 2 × 12–15 |

## Session B: Shoulders, chest and triceps (about 50 min)
| Exercise | Sets × reps |
|---|---|
| Incline DB press | 3 × 8–12 |
| Cable lateral raise | 4 × 12–15 |
| Cable fly (low-to-high) | 3 × 12–15 |

| Exercise | Sets × reps |
|---|---|
| Seated leg curl | 3 × 10–15 |
| Leg extension | 3 × 12–15 |
| Standing or seated calf raise | 4 × 10–15 |

Session C is the one to cut first. Her lower body gets no genuine rest day in REVL, so this is the most expensive session on the menu.

## Placement
- Keep PT clear of about 24 h either side of her densest mixed REVL day and her hinge-led day. Put B on or next to her upper-body-led REVL day, since REVL barely loads her legs that day.
- With 5 REVL days, three PT sessions means at least one lands on a REVL day. Do it as a separate short session, or immediately after class.
- Run A and B on different days from C where possible, so upper and lower don't stack.

## Phase adjustments
| Phase | Change |
|---|---|
| **Build** | Cut to about half-volume (2 sets per exercise), drop session C, and keep RIR 2–3. |
| **Deload week** | Her conditioning isn't deloaded, so don't add high-rep metabolic work. Run A and B at the low end of the volume range. |
| **Peak and testing weeks** | Support work only, with nothing taken near failure. Hypertrophy work pauses. |

## Session count
Booking all three slots is a ceiling, not a quota. My default is to run all three as written, with C at 30–40 min. Review after two weeks. If any recovery marker slips (soreness that lingers, poor sleep, REVL performance dropping), cut C first. The next steps would be shortening A and B, or converting a slot to mobility.

1. **REVL phase and week:** this decides the table above. If she's in Build or Peak, session C goes and the volume halves.
2. **Her track and which weekday is which session:** this decides placement.
3. **Training age, injuries and equipment:** these affect exercise choice.
4. **Screening:** confirm ACSM screening and PAR-Q+ are done. REVL attendance isn't medical clearance.
5. **Nutrition:** I won't give any calorie or protein target. General information only, and she should see a registered dietitian for anything specific. Eating enough is the main limit on muscle gain, so raise it with her early.

Once you have the phase and her weekly schedule, I can scaffold her plan files and fix the days.

rows.response:
**Default recommendation: don't make the sessions harder. Hold the load, keep intensity high, and trim volume a little. Before changing anything, get her nutrition decision made with a registered dietitian (RD).**

**Why harder is the wrong lever**
- Not building muscle is probably not a training-stimulus problem. Muscle gain on a large energy shortfall is limited, and 5 days a week of hard training adds recovery demand on top of that.
- If she's already training 5x a week and stalling, adding volume or intensity is likely to produce fatigue and stalled lifts rather than growth. This is *Applied from the course* (progressive overload and recovery principles) plus *General knowledge* (energy availability limits hypertrophy).
- Framework §1: the mechanism is energy intake against training load. The fix has to act on that, not add more work beside it.

**Scope flag**
- Her intake and deficit are a nutrition decision, so they go to an RD. I'm not giving her a kcal number. Someone has to decide whether the deficit continues at this size, and that person is the RD with her.
- Screen for under-fuelling, because 1400 kcal alongside 5 sessions a week is a flag. Ask about:
  - menstrual changes
  - persistent fatigue or poor sleep
  - illness frequency
  - preoccupation with food
- If any of these are present, refer to a physician or RD. Don't coach around it.

**What to change in the training**
1. **Keep the muscle stimulus, cut the junk.** Hold heavy-ish compound work (roughly 6–12 reps, 2–3 hard sets per movement pattern, 1–3 reps in reserve (RIR) on most sets). Drop extra accessory sets and any "make it harder" finishers or metabolic circuits.
2. **Cap hard days at 3–4.** Make the other 1–2 sessions lighter: technique, mobility, easy cardio. Five maximal sessions isn't recoverable at this intake.
3. **Progression trigger:** when she hits the top of the rep range on all sets at 1–2 RIR for 2 consecutive sessions, add about 5% load (double progression / 2-for-2). If load can't hold or rises, don't add volume. That's the signal the deficit is too big.
4. **Frame the goal honestly.** In a deficit, success is maintaining or slightly gaining strength while fat comes off. If her lifts are flat or rising, she is retaining muscle.

**How to tell if I'm wrong**
- If her lifts are climbing steadily, recovery is good, and the screening questions are clean, then she's likely progressing fine and the real issue is expecting visible muscle gain during weight loss. The fix is expectation-setting and tracking (strength log, girths, photos), not harder sessions.
- If any red flag appears, pause the progression plan and refer.

**Open items that would sharpen this** (answer compactly, e.g. `1B, 2A`):
1. Current weekly structure: 1A full-body ×5 / 1B split ×5 / 1C other / 1D not sure
2. Are her key lifts going up, flat, or down over the last 4–6 weeks? 2A up / 2B flat / 2C down
3. Any of: missed or irregular periods, constant fatigue, poor sleep, frequent illness? 3A none / 3B yes, some / 3C prefer to discuss
4. Has an RD been involved? 4A yes / 4B no

I haven't checked course pages for this reply, so I've left page citations out rather than risk a wrong locator. Tell me if you want me to verify and cite the specific tables, or to scaffold a plan pair for her.

I'm assuming "4x a week" means four REVL sessions. If it's four PT sessions on top of REVL, that is a different problem: it breaks the no-additive-work rule for both clients, and I'd cut it before anything else.

**Client A (24, 9 h sleep, 2 yrs trained)**

- Progress by double progression (2-for-2 rule). Add load once they hit the top of the rep range on both sets for two sessions.
- Real growth work for them is Rebuild/Volume, after the tests.

**Client B (47, shift worker, 8 yrs trained, 5–6 h sleep)**
- Recovery capacity is the limiter, not training stimulus. Eight years trained means a smaller marginal return from extra volume. Short, irregular sleep means the existing REVL load may already be the ceiling.

- A 47-year-old who trains regularly and has no disclosed symptoms or conditions doesn't trigger a medical-clearance block on those facts alone. If any screening flag turns up, that becomes a BLOCKING gap.
- Ask which shifts they work, and whether the 5–6 h is chronic or just this stretch. Sleep timing around the REVL sessions matters. If they're often training on very short sleep after night shifts, drop a REVL session rather than add anything.

**Sleep is the main difference.** Doses can differ, but B's biggest hypertrophy lever is sleep and protein/energy sufficiency. Nutrition stays at general information. Refer to an RD for specifics, and I won't give a kcal number.

2. Which REVL track does each client follow, and which days are the hinge-led and densest ones? (REVL's weekly structure has varied between blocks, so I'm not assuming.)
3. For B: shift pattern, and whether the sleep is chronic?

Here's the plan I'd run. With 5 REVL classes and 3 PT sessions she's at 8 sessions a week, so the plan below is built around keeping that survivable.

## What "most aggressive" means here

I wouldn't stack the most volume you can fit into 3 PT slots. REVL already trains squat and hinge on nearly every day, so lower-body volume is the easiest place to burn her out. The aggressive version puts as much hypertrophy dose as she can recover from into tissue REVL under-serves, and it flexes by REVL phase.

That tissue is horizontal pulling, upper back, rear delts, arms, side delts, and low-axial lower-body isolation (quads, hamstrings, calves). *Applied from the course: REVL reference §6a/§14, plus the hypertrophy band in Table 9-12 and Table 11-10. I haven't re-verified the page numbers this turn.*

## Session count

Eight sessions a week is where I'd put a reduction on the table. She won't drop classes, so the lever is your slots. Don't treat three PT slots as a quota. I'd use all three only when she's fresh in Volume or Rebuild. In Build, drop to 2 sessions, or keep 3 with one as a 30-minute mobility/recovery slot. In Deload and Peak, run 1 hypertrophy session plus support work. If she'd rather keep all three, this still fits as long as the tripwires below are honoured.

## Weekly template (placed by the rules, since I don't have her weekdays)

| Slot | Focus | Placement rule |
|---|---|---|
| **PT-1** | Back/rear delts/biceps. Horizontal pull is her biggest upper-body gap. | Day after the easier conditioning format |
| **PT-2** | Chest/side delts/triceps, with fewer pressing sets than a standard split because REVL presses often. | Away from her densest mixed day and hinge-led day |
| **PT-3** | Low-axial lower-body isolation (leg ext, leg curl, calves) plus arms and carries. | On her upper-body-led REVL day, when her legs get their only offload |

Don't put any PT session within about 24 hours of her densest mixed REVL day. I'm not assigning real weekdays until she confirms which session she does on which day, because REVL has shipped different weekly shapes.

## Dose by REVL phase (general-knowledge dosing heuristics)

| Phase | Direct hard sets per target muscle per week | Effort | PT slots |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Volume / Rebuild** | ~8–10 | RIR 1–2; last isolation set can go to RIR 0 | 3 |
| **Build** | ~5–6 | RIR 2–3, no failure | 2 (or 3 with one recovery slot) |
| **Deload** | Technique and assessment. No high-rep metabolic work, because REVL's conditioning isn't actually deloaded. | Low | 1–2 |
| **Peak** | Maintenance only: ~3–4 sets, no failure, nothing near testing weeks | RIR 3+ | 1 |

Rep range is 6–12 on compounds, per the course's hypertrophy band. Isolation can run 10–15, which is general knowledge. Rest is 30–90 s on isolation and up to ~2 min on heavy compounds. Tempo is controlled, with a 2–3 s eccentric.

**Example Volume-phase PT-1:**
- Chest-supported row, 4 × 6–10
- Neutral-grip pulldown, 3 × 8–12
- Cable rear-delt fly, 3 × 12–15
- Incline DB curl, 3 × 10–12
- Suitcase carry, 3 × 30 m

Chest-supported rows keep the spine unloaded, since the hinge is already the most repeated pattern in her week.

## Progression

Double progression with the 2-for-2 rule. When she hits the top of the rep range at the target RIR for 2 consecutive sessions, add about 5% load (Wk07 Ch11 p7, p20). Progress one variable at a time. Don't add sets until load and reps stall for 2–3 weeks while she's still recovering well.

## Tripwires: cut PT volume before touching REVL

Check readiness at the start of every session: sleep, soreness, REVL performance, mood and appetite. If markers drop, modify in this order:
1. Intensity (push RIR up).
2. Sets.
3. Exercise variant (lower-demand version).
4. Session type (mobility or Zone 1–2).

If markers persist for more than about a week, she needs total load reduced, which includes scaling REVL itself.

## Open items (and how each changes the default)

- **REVL phase and week, track (Perform/Move), and which weekday is which session.** This sets the dose table and session placement. If she's in Build or Peak, start from the lower rows. If it's unknown, start at the Build row.
- **Screening.** REVL attendance isn't medical clearance. Confirm ACSM/PAR-Q+, injuries, age and training age. Any flag blocks me from prescribing beyond what the algorithm permits.
- **Sleep and life stress.** Poor recovery is the most likely limiter on an 8-session week. If it's poor, go to 2 PT slots.
- **Nutrition.** Hypertrophy depends on adequate energy and protein, and the details belong with a registered dietitian. I'm giving no numbers.

## Default recommendation

Start 3 PT sessions as laid out above. Use the Build row of the dose table until you confirm her phase, since that is the conservative end and she's already near the session-count ceiling. Move up to the Volume row only after two good weeks of readiness checks.

**Do one proper PT session a week and turn the second slot into a short one (about 30–40 min) for shoulder and mobility work, an assessment, or easy Zone 2.** Add no pressing, no heavy lower body and no extra conditioning intervals. Revisit when Build starts in week 4.

- REVL 5x plus PT 2x is 7 sessions a week, and she's sore most days while starting a fat-loss push.
- Volume is the phase with the most headroom, but no day of REVL leaves the lower body unloaded (REVL reference §6).
- Her lifts are still rising, so this is not a plateau. Don't replace anything (framework §5).
- Booked slots are a ceiling, not a quota. Reducing PT is a legitimate answer (framework §4).

**2. REVL already supplies the muscle-retention stimulus.**
- Heavy lifting with enough effort is what holds muscle in a deficit.
- Adding more volume, more conditioning of the same type, or a Russian-style strength block would mean a second hard quality on a recovery budget that is already full.
- Not stacking a second strength block follows REVL reference §10. The "less is more" point is general knowledge, not from the ISA course.

**3. The shoulder sets the PT content.**
- The course's shoulder sequence is: open the subacromial space, strengthen the scapular stabilizers (lower traps, rhomboids, serratus anterior, rotator cuff), do controlled anterior strengthening, then reintroduce overhead work in the scapular plane (~30° anterior) with modified ROM (Week 10, Ch 15, p92, which I opened this turn).
- Applied from the course, a PT session could look like this:
  - **Warm-up:** thoracic and shoulder mobility.
  - **Main work:** horizontal rows and face pulls or rear-delt work, 3 sets of 10–12 at RIR 2–3.
  - **Scap/cuff work:** serratus punch and external rotation, 2–3 sets.
  - **Carries:** farmer carries, which REVL barely covers (carries are a small minority of captured sessions).
  - **Optional:** a light scapular-plane press only if it is pain-free.
- Horizontal pulling and carries are the gaps REVL leaves. No more vertical pressing, because REVL already includes it often (a keyword count over the captured posters, lower bound, programme as written, not her sessions).

**4. Fat loss is a nutrition decision I won't put a number on.**
- The course covers general nutrition information and refers detailed deficit and intake decisions to a registered dietitian (Ch 1 scope; Ch 12).
- I'm not giving a deficit figure. Someone has to make that call, and it's her and an RD, not the PT plan.
- Training-wise, general knowledge says strength can usually be held in a deficit while muscle is what suffers, so keep intensity high and don't add volume to compensate.

- Ask whether the shoulder is currently painful or has been assessed. If the pain is sharp, localized, persistent or getting worse, that is a **refer to a physical therapist** matter. Don't clear it yourself, and don't program loaded overhead work to "test" it (framework §7).

- **Shoulder gate (my judgement, not course content):** advance only after two consecutive sessions with no pain during or the next day. Drop back a stage if the shoulder flares.
- **Soreness lasting about a week or more:** cut total load, and consider scaling REVL too. Review sleep and nutrition. If it still doesn't resolve, refer to a physician.
- **In Build (week 4+):** cap PT at half a session, and keep it away from her heaviest day.

**Default recommendation:** for the next 2–3 weeks of Build, make both PT sessions upper-body and tissue-specific, with no loaded squat, hinge or high-eccentric leg work. REVL is already supplying all the leg stimulus they can recover from, so PT should add something different.

## Why this is the call

- **Legs are saturated.** *(REVL reference §6, §14, applied)* No day of a REVL week leaves the lower body unloaded. Even the conditioning days load squat and hinge patterns with lighter implements. Constant soreness is the expected result, and the reference says to change the pattern, not just trim the load.
- **Build leaves little room.** Loads are climbing toward near-maximal and neural headroom is limited. The reference gives half a session or one focused lift as the added dose, and no second heavy exposure.
- **Eight years in is near the ceiling.** In trained lifters, volume matters more than how it's split across days. *(General knowledge: Baz-Valle 2022 suggests 12–20 weekly sets per muscle for hypertrophy, Hamarsland 2021 found no frequency effect when volume was equated. Both are abstract-level evidence from `trained-population-evidence.md`.)* The marginal gain is in tissue REVL under-serves, not in more squats.
- **Where REVL is thin.** *(REVL reference §5–6)* Horizontal pulling, upper back, arms, rear delts, carries and slow unilateral stability. Upper-body work is also concentrated on fewer days than lower-body work.

## Suggested structure (30 min each)

Each session is a 5-min warm-up (thoracic and shoulder mobility, band work), about 20 min of work, then a short cool-down. Intensity is hypertrophy-band: **6–12 reps, 30–90 s rest, RIR 1–3, controlled tempo**. *(Week 07, Ch 11, Table 9-12; I'm relaying this from the skill's digest, not re-opened this turn, so confirm the page before citing it to the client.)*

**PT 1: pull and back emphasis**
1. Chest-supported or cable row, 4 × 8–12
2. Lat pulldown or neutral-grip pull-up variation, 3 × 8–10
3. Rear-delt or face-pull superset with a biceps curl, 3 × 12–15 each
4. Suitcase carry, 3 × 30 m per side

**PT 2: push and shoulders emphasis**
1. Incline DB press, 4 × 8–10
2. Seated DB or landmine press, 3 × 8–12
3. Lateral raise superset with a triceps pressdown, 3 × 12–15 each
4. Optional: seated or slow tempo calf raise, 2–3 × 12–15 (low eccentric cost). Skip it if the calves are part of the soreness.

That is roughly 12–14 hard sets per session across the upper body, which is high for 30 minutes. If time is tight, cut set counts rather than rest.

**Progression trigger (double progression, 2-for-2):** when they hit the top of the rep range on the final set at the target RIR for two consecutive sessions, add about 5% load and drop back to the bottom of the range. *(Week 07, Ch 11, p7 and p20 per the REVL reference; same caveat on page numbers.)* Change one variable at a time.

## Dosing and scheduling rules

- **Placement.** Keep PT away from the day before or after their hinge-led and densest mixed REVL days. I don't know which weekdays those are for this client, so please check (see below).
- **Weekly count.** Three REVL plus two PT is five sessions. That is below the 7–8 threshold at which I'd recommend cutting sessions, so no change is needed.
- **Soreness modification order.** If they arrive sore or flat, cut intensity first, then sets, then swap to a lower-demand variant. If sessions go poorly, convert PT to mobility or easy aerobic work.
- **Persistent markers.** If soreness, poor sleep or falling performance last more than about a week, reduce total load, consider scaling REVL itself, and review sleep and recovery. Refer to a physician if it's unresolved. Sharp or localized pain is a PT or physician referral, not something to train through.

## What to check with the client

Answers to these could change the default:

1. **Which weekday is which REVL session?** This sets where the PT slots go. I'd log the answer in their plan so it isn't re-asked.
2. **How sore, and for how long?** Normal DOMS is 48–72 h. Soreness that never clears points to a recovery problem. In that case drop one PT slot to mobility or easy Zone 1–2 work.
3. **Sleep, stress and protein intake.** For nutrition I can only give general information. Anything detailed, including intake targets, goes to an RD.
4. **Screening on file?** REVL attendance is not medical clearance. Confirm they've done the ACSM screen and PAR-Q+.

**When to revisit.** At Peak, drop to support-only work (no additive strength dose). The Deload week is the better window to assess and add leg work. Return to full volume in Rebuild.

rows.response:
**Default: keep what's working, and add one small, knee-friendly glute dose in the PT sessions. Don't add more heavy lower-body work.**

**Why this plan**
- **Lifts are still going up, so REVL is working.** Soreness on most days is expected in Build. This is a "smallest change" situation, not a reason to overhaul anything (general knowledge, framework §5).
- **Build limits what PT can add.** Loads are climbing and neural headroom is limited, so PT gets about half a session of added dose, not a full block (REVL integration §4 and §12; this is my dosing judgement, not a REVL claim).
- **REVL already loads the hinge and squat patterns very often.** Its programme as written has hinge in most sessions, and no phase gives that pattern a rest. Extra heavy deadlift or squat volume is the most expensive thing you could add. Glute work needs to be a different expression of the pattern, not more of the same.
- **Nadia's age and the knee override the general tables.** Ch 14 (older adults) and Ch 15 (musculoskeletal issues) replace the general FITT-VP values. Check those pages before locking loads.

**Knee pain**
- **Scope:** Deep knee-dominant pain is not something you diagnose or train through. If it's recurring, sharp, or getting worse, refer to a physical therapist or physician. If it's been assessed and cleared, ask what pain-free range they were given.
- **Programming around it:** Pick glute exercises that need little knee flexion, and keep every rep in a pain-free range. Avoid deep squat, deep lunge and loaded deep step-down patterns.
- **Stop rule:** Pain must stay at baseline during and after the session. Any rise in knee pain means you drop that exercise, and persistent pain means referral. Don't test it with a "light rep first".

**PT session 1: glute focus** (placed away from her hinge-led and densest REVL days; confirm those first)
1. Warm-up and glute activation (bridges, banded work): 5–8 min
2. Hip thrust or barbell/DB glute bridge: 3 × 8–12, RIR 2
3. Cable or band hip abduction, or side-lying: 2–3 × 12–15, RIR 1–2
4. 45° back extension or light cable pull-through, **only if** her hinge-led REVL day isn't within about 24 h: 2 × 10–12
5. Optional: shallow step-up to a box height that is pain-free, 2 × 8/side, slow and controlled

This stays inside the hypertrophy band (roughly 6–12 reps, 30–90 s rest, Table 9-12, Wk07 Ch11 p16; verify the page before quoting it to her). I chose hip-dominant work with low eccentric damage on purpose, because she's already sore most days.

**Progression trigger:** Use double progression (2-for-2 rule, Wk07 Ch11 p7, p20). When she gets the top of the rep range at RIR ≥ 2 for two sessions running, add about 5%. If soreness or performance drops, cut sets first, not load.

**PT session 2: don't add more lower-body volume**
Use this slot for the gaps REVL leaves, per §6a:
- Horizontal pulling
- Carries (a suitcase carry is cheap and low-interference)
- Anti-rotation work
- Mobility
- Easy Zone 1–2 aerobic work, if she has no base

If she's beaten up that week, convert it to mobility only. Total load is about 5 sessions a week, so the 7–8 session ceiling isn't a concern yet.

**Check each session**
Run the readiness screen every time (sleep, soreness, last REVL session). If she's flagged, modify in this order: intensity, then volume, then exercise variant, then session type.

**Still open, and how each answer would change the plan**
1. **Which REVL days carry the hinge-led and densest sessions for her, and Perform or Move track?** This decides where session 1 sits.
2. **Has the knee pain been assessed?** If not, I'd put the referral first and keep glute work to bridges and abduction only.
3. **Is the soreness "heavy but recovers by next session" or lingering for days?** If it's lingering, I'd drop session 1 to bridges and abduction at 2 sets.
4. **Any other glute-relevant limits?** Check hip pain, low back history and balance.
5. **Has she done a medical screen (ACSM/PAR-Q+) recently?** REVL attendance doesn't count as clearance.

Anything on the REVL side that I haven't confirmed with Nadia is unestablished, so treat the structure above as a hypothesis until she tells you her actual week.
